segs.text: Monday afternoon in America, Tuesday before dawn in Japan, an H3 rocket is set to leave Tanegashima with a spacecraft called MMX on top. Its job: fly to Mars, orbit its little moon Phobos, land on it, scoop up at least ten grams, and bring them home in 2031. This is Space Now: what is launching, what is up there, what is known, and what is still open.

The time, from JAXA's own launch plan: October 20, 2026, at 4:41 and 3 seconds in the morning, Japan time. That is October 19 at 3:41 in the afternoon, US Eastern. If anything slips, backup days run from October 21 to November 7, each with its own time. The rocket is H3 flight ten, in its heaviest form: two main engines, four solid boosters, the long fairing. JAXA streams it live in English.

Here is the first hour and a bit, as published. Boosters drop at about two minutes. The fairing opens at three minutes seventeen. The first stage separates just before five minutes. The second stage burns, coasts for most of an hour, burns again, and at one hour, eleven minutes and twelve seconds it lets MMX go, already on its way to Mars at about eleven kilometres a second. Then roughly a year of cruise.

The spacecraft weighs 4,480 kilograms at launch, JAXA's figure, and it is built as three modules. A propulsion module does the pushing to Mars and is cast off once its job is done. An exploration module carries the landing legs, the samplers and the science instruments. A return module carries the solar wings, the main antenna, and the capsule that comes back. JAXA leads, with NASA, the French and German space agencies, and ESA.

Why Phobos? It is a lump up to 27 kilometres across, dark as coal, circling about 6,000 kilometres above Mars, once every seven hours and thirty nine minutes. Nobody knows where it came from. One idea: an asteroid that Mars captured; its dark surface looks like one. The other: debris thrown up by a giant impact on Mars, which fits its tidy, near-circular orbit over the equator. Both are still hypotheses. Decades of pictures have not settled it.

A sample can. On Earth, labs can read a Phobos grain for minerals, water, organic matter, isotope ratios and age, far beyond what any orbiter can do. Ryuki Hyodo, a JAXA scientist who models how the moons formed, has explained the test. Debris from a giant impact should be roughly half Martian material, with the easily vaporised elements baked out. A captured asteroid would look like a body from the outer solar system instead, and could carry water and organic matter from out there.

There is a bonus either way. Big impacts on Mars have been spraying rock into space for billions of years, and some of it lands on Phobos. A 2019 model led by Hyodo put Martian material in the top layer at a few hundred parts per million. In ten grams, that could be a few dozen sand-sized grains of Mars, if the grains are about a third of a millimetre. A model estimate, not a measurement. If it holds, a spacecraft would be carrying material from Mars home for the first time, mixed into the Phobos dirt.

The plan, year by year. Late 2027: arrive at Mars and settle into a path that shadows Phobos, a quasi-satellite orbit; MMX would be the first spacecraft to do that. Then months of mapping: shape, gravity, dozens of candidate landing spots. 2029: drop the rover. The landing and sampling: ESA's page says 2030, the German agency's says 2029. Both say the capsule reaches Australia in 2031. Published plan, not a promise.

The rover is called Idefix, built by France and Germany. It weighs 25 kilograms on Earth. On Phobos, where gravity is about one two-thousandth of ours, it weighs about as much as a few coins. MMX lets it fall from about 40 metres. It lands, rights itself and unfolds its four wheels, all on its own. Then about three months of cameras, a Raman spectrometer and a radiometer, testing the ground where the big ship will land.

The landing itself is the hard part. Radio takes up to 44 minutes there and back, so the ship lands by itself on four legs. Two samplers. A corer on a robot arm pushes more than two centimetres into the ground and holds the core with a shape-memory alloy. A pneumatic sampler, provided by NASA, sits by a footpad and uses a puff of nitrogen to blow loose surface grains into a container. Two kinds of dirt: below the surface and on top of it. JAXA's plan calls for two soft landings, about two to three hours on the ground each time.

Along the way the ship measures everything it can: a telescope camera, a wide colour camera, a laser altimeter, an infrared spectrometer from France for minerals and water, NASA's MEGANE, which reads gamma rays and neutrons from cosmic-ray hits to count the elements in the ground, an ion analyser, a dust counter, a radiation monitor, and 8K and 4K cameras built with Japan's broadcaster NHK. Later in the mission it also flies past Deimos, the smaller moon.

So, the ledger. Known: the scheduled launch time, the rocket, the mass, the ten gram target, the three modules, the rover. Published plan: arrive 2027, rover 2029, two short landings, capsule 2031. Open: whether the landing comes in 2029 or 2030, the agencies' pages disagree; how much of Phobos is really Mars; and the big one, where Phobos came from. That last one is the whole point. The answer is in the dirt.

What to watch: liftoff at 3:41 PM Eastern on October 19, boosters off two minutes in, and the moment seventy one minutes later when MMX is on its own. After that, roughly a year of cruise before Mars. We will be following it here, one real mission at a time. Space Now, from Heartbeat Observatory.
